sentences: Six modules ago, Orbit's chatbot apologised four hundred times in one day, because it could not look anything up.
In this last lesson, you look back at what you built, piece by piece, and then look ahead at what to learn next.
After this lesson come the mini project and the final assessment.

slides.title: The loop at the heart of Scout

center.label: Scout
center.sub: an agent, not just a chatbot

note.text: This is the ReAct loop from Module 4. Every agent framework runs some version of it.

sentences: Everything you built turns around one loop.
Scout reads the customer's question, together with what it remembers from the conversation.
It plans: it works out what it needs to know, and which tool could tell it.
It acts by calling a tool, such as get order or track parcel.
It observes the result, including any error, and decides whether it knows enough yet.
Finally it answers within the policy and its limits, or hands over to a person.
That is the react loop from Module 4, and every agent framework runs some version of it.

slides.title: Six modules, one agent

cells: Look things up instead of guessing
Prove it works with a pass rate

note.text: From a chatbot that apologised to an agent that acts, within limits.

sentences: Here is the whole journey in one table.
In Modules 1 and 2 you made your first model call, wrote Scout's system prompt and got clean JSON back.
In Module 3 Scout got tools and the loop that runs them, so it could look things up instead of guessing.
In Module 4 it learned to remember, to search Orbit's policy and to plan.
In Module 5 you assembled the full project and measured it against a test set.
And in Module 6 you added guardrails, an API and logs, so it can serve real customers safely.
That is the path from a chatbot that apologised to an agent that acts, within limits.

slides.title: Scout today, end to end

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: Hi, the storm jacket from order ORB-10588 is too big. Can I send it back for a refund?

messages.label: get_order
messages.text: ORB-10588 · Storm shell jacket, size L · $310 · delivered 5 days ago

messages.label: Guard
messages.text: request_refund for $310: over $200, saved for approval. No money has moved.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: You're within 30 days and return shipping is free. Your $310 refund is waiting for a team member to approve. Or I can swap it for a size M, which is in stock.

aside.label: All in one reply
aside.text: Tools, policy, a guardrail and an honest answer.

sentences: Here is Scout today, handling a request it could not have touched in Module 1.
Owen's storm jacket is too big, and he asks to send it back for a refund.
Scout looks up his order, sees it arrived five days ago, and checks whether a size medium is in stock.
It asks for a three hundred and ten dollar refund, and your guard holds it, because it is over two hundred dollars.
Scout tells Owen the truth: the refund is waiting for approval, and a free exchange is also possible.
Tools, policy, a guardrail and an honest answer, all in one short reply.

slides.title: What to learn next

note.text: The ideas carry over to any provider: OpenAI, Google or open models.

sentences: Where next? Here are four directions that build directly on Scout.
Evaluations at scale: grow your ten test cases into hundreds, and use a model as a grader for answers that have no single right wording.
Retrieval with embeddings: instead of matching words, search Orbit's documents by meaning, with a vector store such as Chroma or pgvector.
More tools through MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for plugging an agent into ready-made tool servers, such as a help desk or a calendar.
And multi-agent systems, for the day one agent is no longer enough.
Everything you learned carries over to other providers, such as OpenAI, Google or open models; only the SDK calls change.
Pick the direction that solves your next real problem, not the most exciting one.

slides.title: Habits to keep
slides.lead: The habits matter more than any one tool or framework.

bullets.text: Scope the agent to one job, and draw it before you code
Write test cases early, and re-run them after every change
Limits, approvals and logs on anything that runs unattended
Keep a person in the loop for what matters

aside.label: And remember
aside.text: Some jobs don't need an agent. A fixed workflow is simpler and cheaper when the steps never change.

sentences: Before the tools, a few habits that will serve you on every agent you build.
Scope the agent to one clear job, and draw its parts before you write any code.
Write test cases early, and re-run them after every change to the prompt, the tools or the model.
Never leave an agent running unattended without step limits, spend limits, approvals and logs.
Keep a person in the loop for decisions that matter, and make it easy for customers to reach one.
And remember Module 1: some jobs do not need an agent at all, and a fixed workflow is simpler and cheaper.

midQuiz.q: In Scout's loop, what happens right after it calls a tool?
options: It answers the customer straight away, whatever the tool said
It observes the result, including any error, and decides what to do next
It starts a fresh conversation with the customer
midQuiz.explain: Read, plan, act, observe: after acting, Scout reads the result or the error and decides whether to call another tool, answer or hand off.
midQuiz.hint: Think of the four words in the loop, in order.

midQuiz.q: Owen asks for a $310 refund. Which part of Scout stops the money moving straight away?
options: The system prompt on its own
The approval guard in your code
midQuiz.explain: needs_approval() checks every refund call before it runs and holds anything over $200 for a person. The prompt asks for it; the code guarantees it.
midQuiz.hint: Which of these still works if the model gets confused?

endQuiz.q: Scout's word-matching search misses policy answers when customers use different words. Which next topic fixes that?
endQuiz.explain: Embeddings let you search by meaning, so "send it back" can find the returns section even though the words differ.
endQuiz.hint: Which topic is about finding text by meaning rather than by matching words?

endQuiz.q: Orbit's help desk tool offers an MCP server. What does MCP give Scout?
options: A cheaper model for simple steps
A standard way to plug in ready-made tools
A way to run without an API key
endQuiz.explain: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting agents to tool servers, so Scout could use the help desk's tools without you writing each one.
endQuiz.hint: MCP is about tools, not models or keys.
